classification.habitat: Open disturbed ground, roadsides and cultivated areas
classification.distribution: Widely distributed in India; the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia draft monograph describes it as occurring commonly throughout the country up to about 900 m.

identification.description: An erect, stiff herb with opposite leaves and characteristic slender terminal spikes bearing small green flowers; mature inflorescences produce rough, persistent bracts that readily cling to passing material.
identification.whole_plant: Erect herb, commonly about 0.1–0.9 m in the pharmacopoeial description, with branched upper portions and terminal spikes.
identification.root: Slender taproot; detailed organoleptic authentication should follow pharmacopoeial standards.
identification.stem: Erect, branched, longitudinally striated stem; young portions may be hairy.
identification.leaf: Opposite, simple, petiolate leaves; broadly ovate to elliptic and commonly hairy, with an acute to obtuse apex.
identification.flower: Small greenish flowers densely arranged on elongated terminal spikes; bracts are conspicuous and stiff.
identification.fruit: Small utricle enclosed by persistent perianth/bracts; the mature spike is rough and prickly to touch.
identification.seed: Small, dark to brownish seed enclosed within the persistent floral structures.
identification.bark: Not a distinct bark-bearing woody drug; stem characters are used for practical identification.
identification_points: Erect herb with terminal slender spikes
Small greenish flowers densely arranged on spikes
Persistent stiff bracts give the inflorescence its prickly character
Whole plant is the pharmacopoeial drug Apāmārga Pañcāṅga

modern_information.evidence_summary: The official pharmacopoeial draft identifies Apāmārga Pañcāṅga as the dried whole plant of Achyranthes aspera L. Traditional medicinal uses are documented in AYUSH educational material, but individual claims should not be treated as proof of clinical efficacy.
modern_information.safety_notes: This dossier is educational. Traditional indications and pharmacopoeial identity do not establish efficacy for a specific patient or replace diagnosis and treatment.

student.quick_revision: Apāmārga is Achyranthes aspera L. of Amaranthaceae; the official pharmacopoeial drug is the dried whole plant (Pañcāṅga), recognized by its erect habit, opposite leaves and characteristic terminal spikes.

teaching_points: Demonstrate whole-plant authentication before discussing therapeutic claims.
Distinguish pharmacopoeial drug identity from generic herbal uses found online.
Discuss why the persistent spike/bracts are useful practical characters.
discussion_points: Compare Apamarga with other Amaranthaceae weeds during herbarium practicals.
Explain the difference between classical action terms and modern pharmacological evidence.
practical_points: Use authenticated herbarium material for identification.
Record leaf arrangement, indumentum, stem habit and inflorescence before drying.
For crude-drug practicals, compare material with the current pharmacopoeial monograph.

doctor.quick_reference: Whole plant (Pañcāṅga) of Achyranthes aspera L.; classical profile includes Katu-Tikta rasa, Laghu-Tikshna guna, Ushna virya and Katu vipaka. Use formulation-specific authoritative references for prescribing.
